results.title: Saddam Haftar, Chad’s president push deeper security cooperation
results.description: Saddam Haftar, Chad’s president push deeper security cooperation Eastern Libyan authorities have increasingly focused on securing the southern frontier, arguing that instability across neighbouring countries has heightened security risks. Monday 27/07/2026 Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the eastern-based Libyan National Army, shakes hands with Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno in N’Djamena, July 26, 2026. BENGHAZI/N’DJAMENA Saddam Haftar, deputy commander of the eastern-based Libyan National Army, held talks with Chadian President Mahamat Idriss Deby Itno on Sunday on expanding military and security cooperation, as both sides sought closer coordination against growing cross-border threats along their shared frontier. Haftar, who arrived in N’Djamena on an official visit, met Deby at the presidential palace, where they discussed regional developments and ways to deepen bilateral cooperation in areas serving the strategic interests of both countries, according to a statement issued by the eastern-based General Command. Haftar said the forces under his command remained committed to strengthening military and security cooperation with Chad to confront shared challenges and reinforce regional stability. Deby praised the role played by eastern Libyan forces in supporting regional security and stability, the statement said. The meeting builds on expanding military coordination between eastern Libya and Chad after both sides agreed earlier this year to implement a joint border security mechanism. That followed the creation of a joint force in late 2025 tasked with combating smuggling, cross-border crime and other security threats. The two countries share a largely remote desert frontier stretching more than 1,000 kilometres that has long been used by smugglers, armed groups and migrants travelling across the Sahel and North Africa. Eastern Libyan authorities have increasingly focused on securing the southern frontier, arguing that instability across neighbouring countries has heightened security risks. Libya remains divided between rival administrations. The internationally-recognised Government of National Unity, headed by Prime Minister Abdulhamid Dbeibah, governs western Libya from Tripoli, while the eastern-based administration appointed by the House of Representatives operates from Benghazi under Prime Minister Osama Hammad and is backed by Khalifa Haftar’s forces. The United Nations has spent years attempting to broker a political settlement and organise national elections aimed at ending Libya’s prolonged political split following the 2011 uprising that toppled Muammar Gadhafi.
